title: How do you choose a shard key, and what goes wrong with a bad one: why does an uneven key create a HOT SHARD (one node gets disproportionate data/traffic and caps the whole system's scalability), and why must a good shard key both distribute data evenly AND keep common queries localized to a single shard?
shortTitle: How do you choose a shard key, and what goes wrong with a bad one
keyPoints: The shard key is the single most consequential decision in sharding; it is effectively permanent.
A good shard key must simultaneously distribute data evenly AND keep common queries on one shard.
A hot shard is one node that receives disproportionate load, capping the entire cluster's throughput.
Low-cardinality keys (like country) dump most rows on one shard; monotonic keys (like auto-increment) send all new writes to one shard.
Poor locality scatters common queries to every shard (scatter-gather), making even simple queries slow.
Customer ID is often the best banking shard key: high cardinality for even spread plus natural filter for per-customer queries.
The shard key is also the transaction boundary: single-shard operations keep ACID, cross-shard do not.

s1_definition.oneliner: A good shard key spreads data and traffic evenly AND keeps common queries on one shard; a bad one creates a hot shard that becomes the bottleneck capping the whole system.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Shard key** – The field whose value determines which shard a row lives on; once data is distributed, changing it requires a painful re-shard.
- **Even distribution** – Data and request traffic spread roughly equally across all shards so no node is overloaded.
- **Query locality** – Common queries filter on the shard key and hit a single shard instead of scatter-gathering to all.
- **Hot shard** – One node receiving disproportionate data or traffic that saturates its resources and caps the cluster.
- **Transaction boundary** – Single-shard operations keep ACID; cross-shard operations need distributed coordination.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India assigns each customer to a counter based on some rule. A good rule spreads customers evenly so every counter is equally busy, and keeps each customer's related business at one counter. A bad rule, like sending everyone who opened an account today to the same counter, piles a huge crowd at that one counter. That overloaded counter is the hot shard: it caps how fast the whole branch can serve customers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Shard Key Decision:

  Good Key (customer_id):
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ customer_id = SAV2001       │ -> hash -> Shard 2
  │ All of Rajesh's data:       │
  │   accounts, transactions,   │
  │   statements                │
  │ Common query: WHERE cust=X  │ -> hits ONE shard
  └─────────────────────────────┘

  Bad Key (country):
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ country = 'India'           │ -> Shard 0
  │ 90% of all customers!       │ -> HOT SHARD
  │ Shard 0 saturated.          │
  │ Shards 1,2,3 nearly empty.  │
  └─────────────────────────────┘

  Bad Key (auto-increment ID with range):
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ ID 1-1M -> Shard 0 (cold)  │
  │ ID 1M-2M -> Shard 1 (cold) │
  │ ID 2M-3M -> Shard 2 (cold) │
  │ ID 3M-4M -> Shard 3 (HOT)  │ <- all new writes here
  └─────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The shard key is the field that decides which shard a row lives on, and it is the single most consequential decision in sharding because it is effectively permanent. A good shard key must do two things at once: distribute data and traffic evenly so no shard becomes a bottleneck, and keep common queries localized to one shard so they do not scatter-gather.

A hot shard is one node receiving disproportionate load. It caps the entire cluster because the system is only as fast as its busiest shard, and adding more shards does not help. Hot shards come from low-cardinality keys (country), monotonic keys (auto-increment ID), or popularity-correlated keys (celebrity merchant). Poor locality scatters even simple queries to every shard.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj first sharded by opening date (monotonic), creating a hot shard for new accounts. They tried region, but most customers were in one state. Switching to customer_id fixed both: it spread evenly under hashing and kept per-customer queries on one shard. The key is also the transaction boundary: single-shard operations keep ACID while cross-shard ones need a Saga.

Remember one sentence: a good shard key must spread data evenly so no node becomes a hot shard AND keep common queries on one shard, and in banking customer_id usually wins because a bad key creates a bottleneck that no amount of extra shards can fix.
